claim: Long-term adult stem cells sustain tissue regeneration throughout the lifetime of an organism.
source: Long-term adult stem cells sustain tissue regeneration throughout the lifetime of an organism.
evidence: This is a general statement about stem cell function supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Long-term adult stem cells were hypothesized to originate from embryonic progenitor cells that acquire long-term self-renewal ability and multipotency at the end of organogenesis.
source: They were hypothesized to originate from embryonic progenitor cells that acquire long-term self-renewal ability and multipotency at the end of organogenesis.
evidence: This statement references a hypothesis in the field, supported by citation to Slack, 2008 in the Introduction.

claim: Long-term hair follicle stem cells arise from embryonic progenitor cells occupying a niche location that is defined by attenuated Wnt/β-catenin signaling.
source: Here, we discovered that long-term hair follicle stem cells arise from embryonic progenitor cells occupying a niche location that is defined by attenuated Wnt/β-catenin signaling.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by multiple experimental results including lineage tracing, RNA-seq, and genetic manipulation experiments.

claim: Hair follicle initiation is marked by placode formation, which depends on the activation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling.
source: Hair follicle initiation is marked by placode formation, which depends on the activation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple previous studies (van Genderen et al., 1994; Gat et al., 1998; Huelsken et al., 2001; Andl et al., 2002; Jamora et al., 2003; Millar et al., 1999; Reddy et al., 2001; Fu and Hsu, 2013) as referenced in the Introduction.

claim: A region with attenuated Wnt/β-catenin signaling emerges in the upper follicle soon after placode formation.
source: Soon afterwards, a region with attenuated Wnt/β-catenin signaling emerges in the upper follicle.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing differential expression of Wnt pathway genes and TOPGAL reporter experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Embryonic progenitor cells residing in the region with attenuated Wnt/β-catenin signaling gain expression of adult stem cell markers and become definitive long-term hair follicle stem cells at the end of organogenesis.
source: Embryonic progenitor cells residing in this region gain expression of adult stem cell markers and become definitive long-term hair follicle stem cells at the end of organogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing experiments with Nfatc1-CreER and Lgr5-CreER mice shown in Figure 1 and long-term tracing in Figure 6.

claim: Attenuation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling is a prerequisite for hair follicle stem cell specification because it suppresses Sox9, which is required for stem cell formation.
source: Attenuation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling is a prerequisite for hair follicle stem cell specification because it suppresses Sox9, which is required for stem cell formation.
evidence: This is supported by gain-of-function experiments with Exon3-Ctnnb1 mice (Figure 5) showing loss of Sox9 expression and HFSC specification, and loss-of-function experiments showing expanded Sox9 expression.

claim: Adult stem cells in hair follicles are located at the so-called 'outer bulge region'.
source: Adult SCs in hair follicles (HFs) are located at the so-called 'outer bulge region'.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field supported by multiple citations (Paus et al., 1999; Morris et al., 2004; Tumbar et al., 2004; Blanpain et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2009; Hsu et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2012).

claim: The bulge region constitutes the bottom of the permanent portion of a hair follicle.
source: The bulge region constitutes the bottom of the permanent portion of a HF.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about hair follicle structure.

claim: The bulge region contains two layers of epithelial cells: the CD34- inner layer niche cells and the CD34+ outer layer stem cells.
source: It contains two layers of epithelial cells: the CD34- inner layer niche cells and the CD34+ outer layer stem cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bulge structure supported by previous literature.

claim: The bulge structure is only formed when hair follicles enter the first postnatal telogen (resting phase).
source: Although HFs begin to develop in the embryo, the bulge structure is only formed when HFs enter the first postnatal telogen (resting phase); this delineates the end of organogenesis and the emergence of the adult SC niche (Paus et al., 1999; Morris et al., 2004; Tumbar et al., 2004; Blanpain et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2009; Hsu et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Activation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling in basal epithelial cells by locally expressed Wnt ligands is both necessary and sufficient to induce placode formation.
source: Activation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling in basal epithelial cells by locally expressed Wnt ligands is both necessary and sufficient to induce placode formation (van Genderen et al., 1994; Gat et al., 1998; Huelsken et al., 2001; Andl et al., 2002; Jamora et al., 2003; Millar et al., 1999; Reddy et al., 2001; Fu and Hsu, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Placode epithelial cells express the Wnt inhibitor Dkk concomitant with Wnt ligand production.
source: Concomitant with Wnt ligand production, placode epithelial cells also express the Wnt inhibitor Dkk (Bazzi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bazzi et al., 2007.

claim: The combination of the short-range activator Wnt and the long-range inhibitor DKK function in a reaction-diffusion mechanism to suppress Wnt/β-catenin signaling in cells surrounding existing placodes, thereby regulating hair follicle spacing.
source: The combination of the short-range activator Wnt and the long-range inhibitor DKK function in a reaction-diffusion mechanism to suppress Wnt/β-catenin signaling in cells surrounding existing placodes, thereby regulating HF spacing (Sick et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sick et al., 2006.

claim: Inhibition of BMP signaling through the dermal BMP inhibitor Noggin is necessary for placode morphogenesis.
source: Contrary to the required activation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling, inhibition of BMP signaling through the dermal BMP inhibitor Noggin is necessary for placode morphogenesis (Jamora et al., 2003; Botchkarev et al., 1999; Kobielak et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Shh is expressed by placode epithelial cells.
source: Shh is expressed by placode epithelial cells (Oro et al., 1997; St-Jacques et al., 1998; Morgan et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the absence of Shh, dermal condensate fails to aggregate and hair follicle development arrests at the placode stage instead of developing into the hair germ.
source: In the absence of Shh, dermal condensate fails to aggregate and HF development arrests at the placode stage instead of developing into the hair germ.
evidence: This is supported by citations to St-Jacques et al., 1998; Oro and Higgins, 2003; Levy et al., 2007.

claim: Guard hairs, as the first hair follicles to appear in the embryonic backskin, are uniquely dependent on Eda/EdaR signaling.
source: Guard hairs, as the first HFs to appear in the embryonic backskin, are uniquely dependent on Eda/EdaR signaling (Laurikkala et al., 2002; Mustonen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Eda is a Wnt signaling target.
source: Eda, which is itself a Wnt signaling target (Laurikkala et al., 2001), can induce the expression of BMP inhibitors and Shh in guard hair (Pummila et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Laurikkala et al., 2001 and Pummila et al., 2007.

claim: Eda can induce the expression of BMP inhibitors and Shh in guard hair.
source: Eda, which is itself a Wnt signaling target (Laurikkala et al., 2001), can induce the expression of BMP inhibitors and Shh in guard hair (Pummila et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pummila et al., 2007.

claim: Placode progenitor cells generate all cells in adult hair follicles.
source: Placode progenitor cells generate all cells in adult HFs (Levy et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Levy et al., 2007.

claim: Putative hair follicle stem cells are present in postnatal developing hair follicles as slow cycling cells.
source: Previous studies using label-retaining methods demonstrated that putative HFSCs are present in postnatal developing HFs as slow cycling cells, and it was shown that their specification requires the transcription factor Sox9 (Nowak et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nowak et al., 2008.

claim: Hair follicle stem cell specification requires the transcription factor Sox9.
source: Previous studies using label-retaining methods demonstrated that putative HFSCs are present in postnatal developing HFs as slow cycling cells, and it was shown that their specification requires the transcription factor Sox9 (Nowak et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nowak et al., 2008.

claim: Placode cells already express adult hair follicle stem cell markers such as Lhx2 and Sox9, although in a largely non-overlapping pattern.
source: Intriguingly, placode cells already express adult HFSC markers such as Lhx2 and Sox9, although in a largely non-overlapping pattern.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rhee et al., 2006; Horsley et al., 2008; Vidal et al., 2005.

claim: The hair follicle stem cell marker Nfatc1 appears in the hair peg stage.
source: Another HFSC marker, Nfatc1, appears in the subsequent hair peg (Rhee et al., 2006; Horsley et al., 2008; Vidal et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Tail skin hair follicles are arranged in triplets.
source: Unlike un-patterned back skin HFs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), tail skin HFs are arranged in triplets, and the growth of two secondary outer follicles is typically initiated next to a primary central follicle after it has already developed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the description in the text and images in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The growth of two secondary outer follicles is typically initiated next to a primary central follicle after it has already developed in tail skin.
source: Unlike un-patterned back skin HFs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), tail skin HFs are arranged in triplets, and the growth of two secondary outer follicles is typically initiated next to a primary central follicle after it has already developed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the description in the text and images in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Shh-expressing placode cells can become hair follicle stem cells.
source: When we used inducible Shh-CreER::Rosa-stop-mTmG (Harfe et al., 2004) mice to label Shh-expressing cells in either the placode or the hair germ, we found that in both cases Shh+ progenitors cells can become HFSCs (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing experiments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Shh-expressing hair germ cells can become hair follicle stem cells.
source: When we used inducible Shh-CreER::Rosa-stop-mTmG (Harfe et al., 2004) mice to label Shh-expressing cells in either the placode or the hair germ, we found that in both cases Shh+ progenitors cells can become HFSCs (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing experiments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Shh-expressing hair peg cells lost the ability to form hair follicle stem cells and mostly contributed to differentiated lineages.
source: Unexpectedly, Shh-expressing hair peg cells lost the ability to form HFSCs and mostly contributed to differentiated lineages (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing experiments shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: Progenies of Shh-expressing placode cells separate into two different populations: the population still expressing Shh lose the potential to form hair follicle stem cells, while the cells with down regulated Shh expression in hair peg can presumably still become hair follicle stem cells.
source: Since Shh-expressing placode cells generate the majority of cells in hair peg, including those still expressing Shh, this intriguing change in cell fate indicates that progenies of Shh-expressing placode cells separate into two different populations: the population still expressing Shh loose the potential to form HFSCs, while the cells with down regulated Shh expression in hair peg can presumably still become HFSCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lineage tracing data showing different outcomes for Shh+ cells at different stages.

claim: Lgr5 and Nfatc1 first begin to be expressed in hair peg, with complementary patterns to that of Shh.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, two adult HFSC markers, Lgr5 and Nfatc1, first begin to be expressed in hair peg, with complementary patterns to that of Shh (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing and imaging data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Nfatc1-expressing cells first appear at the upper hair peg and remain relatively dormant there, without actively contributing to hair follicle down growth.
source: Using Nfatc1-CreER::Rosa-stop-mTmG mice (Tian et al., 2014), we found that Nfatc1-expressing cells first appear at the upper hair peg and remain relatively dormant there, without actively contributing to HF down growth (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing experiments shown in Figure 1F.

claim: At the end of organogenesis, Nfatc1-expressing hair peg cells become the sebaceous gland above bulge and most of the hair follicle stem cells.
source: Then, at the end of organogenesis, Nfatc1-expressing hair peg cells become the sebaceous gland above bulge and most of the HFSCs (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing experiments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Lgr5-expressing cells appear first in the middle portion of the hair peg.
source: Using Lgr5-GFP-CreER::Rosa-stop-tdTomato mice (Jaks et al., 2008), we found that Lgr5-expressing cells appear first in the middle portion of the hair peg.
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing experiments with Lgr5-GFP-CreER mice.

claim: Lgr5-expressing hair peg cells eventually become hair follicle stem cells in the lower bulge and secondary hair germ cells below the bulge.
source: They eventually become HFSCs in the lower bulge and secondary hair germ cells below the bulge (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing experiments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Hair follicle stem cells originate from progenitor cells in hair peg that lose Shh expression but gain the expression of adult stem cell markers.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that HFSCs originate from progenitor cells in hair peg that lose Shh expression but gain the expression of adult stem cell markers (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lineage tracing experiments presented in Figure 1.

claim: Hair peg stem cell precursors are distinguished from the broader placode and hair germ cells in that they stop further development once they are specified.
source: The hair peg SC precursors are distinguished from the broader placode and hair germ cells in that they stop further development once they are specified.
evidence: This is supported by the observation that Nfatc1+ cells remain dormant without contributing to HF down growth (Figure 1F).

claim: During subsequent hair follicle down growth, hair peg stem cell precursors remain dormant in their original position until the end of organogenesis.
source: During subsequent HF down growth, these cells remain dormant in their original position until the end of organogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing data showing Nfatc1+ cells staying in place (Figure 1F).

claim: At the end of organogenesis, hair peg stem cell precursors incorporate into the outer layer of the bulge and become hair follicle stem cells.
source: At that point, they incorporate into the outer layer of the bulge and become HFSCs.
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing experiments showing Nfatc1+ cells becoming bulge stem cells (Figure 1D).

claim: Following complete ablation of Nfatc1-CreER-labeled cells, de novo bulge formation occurs at the end of organogenesis.
source: Following complete ablation of Nfatc1-CreER-labeled cells, we observed de novo bulge formation at the end of organogenesis (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by laser ablation experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: The newly formed bulge after ablation of Nfatc1+ cells has the same number of stem cells as the control hair follicles.
source: The newly formed bulge even had the same number of SCs as the control HFs (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Almost all stem cells in neighboring control hair follicles were tdTomato positive after Nfatc1-CreER labeling, while the de novo formed stem cells in the ablated hair follicles were all tdTomato negative.
source: Under this condition, almost all SCs in neighboring control HFs were tdTomato positive, while the de novo formed SCs in the ablated HFs were all tdTomato negative (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by quantification and imaging shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The de novo formed hair follicle stem cells after ablation were functional as indicated by their ability to support hair follicle down growth.
source: Importantly, the de novo formed HFSCs were functional as indicated by their ability to support HF down growth (Figure 2F-I and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by imaging and quantification shown in Figure 2F-I.

claim: Niche location in hair peg determines hair follicle stem cell fate.
source: These results indicate that niche location in hair peg determines HFSC fate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ablation experiments showing that new cells at the same location can become HFSCs.

claim: Among genes that were expressed ≥2-fold more in Shh+ cells than in Nfatc1+ cells, genes of the Wnt signaling pathway were enriched prominently.
source: Based on DAVID functional gene annotation analysis (Dennis et al., 2003), among genes that were expressed ≥2-fold more in Shh+ cells than in Nfatc1+ cells, we found that genes of the Wnt signaling pathway were enriched prominently (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and Gene Ontology analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Several canonical Wnts and some well-known Wnt/β-catenin target genes, including Axin2, were highly expressed in Shh+ cells.
source: Several canonical Wnts and some well-known Wnt/β-catenin target genes, including Axin2, were highly expressed in Shh+ cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Axin2, Wnt10b, Wnt3, and Lef1 were all expressed at higher levels in Shh+ cells than in Nfatc1+ hair peg cells.
source: Using either real-time PCR or in situ hybridization, we confirmed that Axin2, Wnt10b, Wnt3, and Lef1 were all expressed at higher levels in Shh+ cells than in Nfatc1+ hair peg cells (Figure 3E-G).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR and in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3E-G.

claim: Starting in the placode stage and persisting through to subsequent development stages, Shh+ cells showed consistent co-localization with β-gal+ cells in TOPGAL Wnt/β-catenin signal reporter mice.
source: Starting in the placode stage and persisting through to subsequent development stages, Shh+ cells showed consistent co-localization with β-gal+ cells (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by imaging of TOPGAL reporter mice shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The hair peg niche position is associated with an absence of Wnt/β-catenin signaling.
source: These results suggest that the hair peg niche position is associated with an absence of Wnt/β-catenin signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from RNA-seq and reporter data showing lack of Wnt signaling in Nfatc1+ cells.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signal responsive cells in placode give rise to most of the hair follicle stem cells.
source: As expected, Wnt/β-catenin signal responsive cells in placode give rise to most of the HFSCs (Figure 4A,B) (Huelsken et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing with Axin2-CreER mice shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: The correlation between Wnt/β-catenin signal responsive cells and hair follicle stem cell formation was dramatically decreased at the hair germ stage, and even further decreased at the hair peg stage.
source: This clear correlation at the placode stage was dramatically decreased at the hair germ stage, and even further decreased at the hair peg stage.
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing with Axin2-CreER mice at different stages shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Only a very small proportion of hair follicle stem cells came from Axin2+ hair peg cells; the majority of hair follicle stem cells came from Axin2- hair peg cells.
source: Only a very small proportion of HFSCs came from Axin2+ hair peg cells; the majority of HFSCs came from Axin2- hair peg cells (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing quantification shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: From the placode stage to the hair peg stage, cells that maintain active Wnt/β-catenin signaling have dramatically decreased potential to form hair follicle stem cells.
source: This suggests that from the placode stage to the hair peg stage, cells that maintain active Wnt/β-catenin signaling have dramatically decreased potential to form HFSC.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Axin2 lineage tracing data.

claim: Almost all the hair follicle cells were Gli1+ in all the early developmental stages examined.
source: Almost all the HF cells were Gli1+ in all the early developmental stages examined (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing with Gli1-CreER mice shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Id2 only became active in terminally differentiated hair bulb cells after future hair follicle stem cell fate had been specified.
source: Id2 only became active in terminally differentiated hair bulb cells after future HFSC fate had been specified (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing with Id2-CreER mice shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Attenuated Wnt/β-catenin signaling is uniquely associated with the hair follicle stem cell-inducing niche location in hair peg.
source: The results from these experiments indicate that attenuated Wnt/β-catenin signaling is uniquely associated with the HFSC-inducing niche location in hair peg (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing lineage tracing results of different signaling pathways.

claim: Activation of canonical Wnt/β-catenin signaling in Nfatc1+ cells was confirmed by nuclear β-catenin staining.
source: Activation of canonical Wnt/β-catenin signaling in Nfatc1+ cells was confirmed by nuclear β-catenin staining (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Initial hair follicle development was normal in exon3-Ctnnb1 heterozygous mice.
source: Initial HF development was normal in exon3-Ctnnb1 heterozygous (Het) mice.
evidence: This is an observation from the conditional activation experiments.

claim: After morphogenesis, rather than entering a new hair cycle like the wild-type, the hair shafts of exon3-Ctnnb1 heterozygous mice were shed.
source: However, after morphogenesis, rather than entering a new hair cycle like the WT, the hair shafts of Het mice were shed (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by imaging shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Bulge formation was completely abolished in exon3-Ctnnb1 heterozygous mice.
source: Section staining revealed that bulge formation was completely abolished in exon3-Ctnnb1 Het mice.
evidence: This is supported by section staining shown in Figure 5C-E.

claim: There were disorganized Keratin6+ cells where the bulge should have been in exon3-Ctnnb1 heterozygous mice, but there were no cells expressing the hair follicle stem cell markers CD34 or Sox9.
source: There were disorganized Keratin6+ cells where the bulge should have been, but there were no cells expressing the HFSC markers CD34 or Sox9 (Figure 5C-E).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining shown in Figure 5C-E.

claim: When Wnt/β-catenin signaling was increased in hair peg niche-occupying cells, neither hair follicle stem cells nor the bulge niche formed at the end of organogenesis.
source: Thus, when Wnt/β-catenin signaling was increased in hair peg niche-occupying cells, neither HFSCs nor the bulge niche formed at the end of organogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the exon3-Ctnnb1 experiments.

claim: With increased time, the exon3-Ctnnb1 heterozygous mice started to generate new hair coats with normal bulges and hair follicle stem cells that expressed CD34 and Sox9.
source: Interestingly, with increased time, the exon3-Ctnnb1 Het mice started to generate new hair coats with normal bulges and HFSCs that expressed CD34 and Sox9 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: This is supported by imaging shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Cells expressing exon3-Ctnnb1 have spontaneously disappeared from hair follicles, and the remaining mosaic wild-type cells organized into a de novo niche after entering the normal hair cycle process.
source: Cells expressing exon3-Ctnnb1 have spontaneously disappeared from HFs, and the remaining mosaic WT cells organized into a de novo niche after entering the normal hair cycle process (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by genotyping data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Attenuated Wnt/β-catenin signaling is required for hair follicle stem cell fate specification.
source: These observation further supports our conclusion that attenuated Wnt/β-catenin signaling is required for HFSC fate specification.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the recovery of normal HFSCs after loss of exon3-Ctnnb1 expressing cells.

claim: Sox9 is an essential intrinsic factor that is required for hair follicle stem cell formation.
source: Sox9 is known to be an essential intrinsic factor that is required for HFSC formation.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Nowak et al., 2008.

claim: Ablation of epithelial Sox9 completely blocks hair follicle stem cell specification.
source: Ablation of epithelial Sox9 completely blocks HFSC specification (Nowak et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nowak et al., 2008.

claim: In normal developing hair follicles, Sox9 expressing cells and Wnt/β-catenin signal responsive cells are mutually exclusive.
source: To determine if the canonical Wnt signal suppresses Sox9 expression in HFs, first we observed that in normal developing HFs, Sox9 expressing cells and Wnt/β-catenin signal responsive cells are mutually exclusive (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by imaging of TOPGAL reporter mice shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Soon after activation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling in Nfatc1+ cells, small protrusions from hair follicles that were positive for nuclear β-catenin had completely absent Sox9 expression, while cells immediately next to these protrusions express Sox9.
source: Second, soon after activation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling in Nfatc1+ cells, we observed small protrusions from HFs that were positive for nuclear β-catenin. Sox9 expression in these small protrusions was completely absent, while cells immediately next to these protrusions express Sox9 (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by imaging shown in Figure 5G.

claim: In the Wnt/β-catenin loss of function mutant, hair follicle development is defective but Sox9 expression is expanded to the extent that all remaining cells in hair follicles express Sox9.
source: Lastly, in the Wnt/β-catenin loss of function mutant (K14-rtTA::teto-Cre::Ctnnb1fl/fl) (Nguyen et al., 2006; Perl et al., 2002), HF development is defective but Sox9 expression is expanded to the extent that all remaining cells in HFs express Sox9 (Figure 5H-J).
evidence: This is supported by imaging shown in Figure 5H-J.

claim: The Wnt/β-catenin signaling suppresses Sox9 expression in hair follicles.
source: These results suggest that the Wnt/β-catenin signaling suppresses Sox9 expression in HFs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including reporter mice, gain-of-function, and loss-of-function experiments.

claim: The requirement for attenuation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling as a prerequisite for hair follicle stem cell specification is related to enabling Sox9 expression.
source: Given that the loss of Sox9 expression completely blocks HFSC specification, the requirement for attenuation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling as a prerequisite for HFSC specification is related to enabling Sox9 expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the relationship between Wnt signaling and Sox9 expression.

claim: Hair shaft formation is aborted in K14-rtTA::teto-Cre::Ctnnb1fl/fl mice.
source: It is noteworthy that hair shaft formation is aborted in K14-rtTA::teto-Cre::Ctnnb1fl/fl mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by imaging shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: Epithelial Wnt/β-catenin signaling is required for progenitor cell differentiation.
source: This indicates that epithelial Wnt/β-catenin signaling is required for progenitor cell differentiation, and may further explain why activation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling prevents HFSC formation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that loss of β-catenin blocks hair shaft formation.

claim: A small portion of hair follicle stem cells come from hair peg cells maintaining active Wnt/β-catenin signaling, while the majority of hair follicle stem cells come from progenitor cells with attenuated Wnt/β-catenin signaling in hair peg.
source: This suggests that there are two origins of HFSCs: a small portion of HFSCs come from hair peg cells maintaining active Wnt/β-catenin signaling, while the majority HFSCs come from progenitor cells with attenuated Wnt/β-catenin signaling in hair peg.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Axin2 lineage tracing data showing ~15% of HFSCs come from Axin2+ cells.

claim: Approximately 15% of hair follicle stem cells in the first telogen originated from Axin2+ hair peg cells.
source: Consistent with results presented in Figure 4A, ~15% of HFSCs in the first telogen originated from Axin2+ hair peg cells.
evidence: This is supported by quantification from lineage tracing experiments.

claim: In the first growth phase (anagen) following the first telogen, hair follicle stem cells derived from Axin2+ hair peg cells contributed to both outer root sheath cells and to matrix differentiating cells.
source: In the first growth phase (anagen) following the first telogen, these HFSCs contributed to both outer root sheath (ORS) cells and to matrix differentiating cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing imaging shown in Figure 6B.

claim: After two full hair cycles, in the third telogen, Axin2+ hair peg cell formed hair follicle stem cells have been mostly exhausted.
source: Of note, after two full hair cycles, in the third telogen, Axin2+ hair peg cell formed HFSCs have been mostly exhausted (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing quantification shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Sox9+ hair peg precursor cells were the origin of most of the hair follicle stem cells at the first telogen.
source: On the contrary, Sox9+ hair peg precursor cells were the origin of most of the HFSCs at the first telogen.
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing with Sox9-CreER mice.

claim: During the first anagen, hair follicle stem cells derived from Sox9+ hair peg cells contributed preferentially to outer root sheath rather than to the differentiated lineages in the matrix.
source: During the first anagen, these HFSCs contributed preferentially to ORS rather than to the differentiated lineages in the matrix.
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing imaging shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Instead of decreasing, hair follicle stem cells originated from Sox9+ hair peg cells persisted and expanded after one round of hair cycle to become essentially all of the hair follicle stem cells in the bulge and most of the secondary hair germ cells below the bulge.
source: Instead of decreasing, HFSCs originated from Sox9+ hair peg cells persisted and expanded after one round of hair cycle to become essentially all of the HFSCs in the bulge and most of the secondary hair germ cells below the bulge.
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing imaging shown in Figure 6D.

claim: For the second anagen, the labeled hair follicle stem cells from Sox9+ precursors generate all of the downstream lineages including outer root sheath, matrix, and hair shaft cells.
source: For the second anagen, the labeled HFSCs generate all of the downstream lineages including, ORS, matrix, and hair shaft cells (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing imaging shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Embryonic Wnt/β-catenin signaling diminishes the long-term potential of hair follicle stem cells.
source: These results suggest that embryonic Wnt/β-catenin signaling diminishes the long-term potential of HFSCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the long-term fate of Axin2+ versus Sox9+ derived HFSCs.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signaling is required for terminal differentiation of the hair shaft.
source: We have shown that Wnt/β-catenin signaling is required for terminal differentiation of the hair shaft.
evidence: This is supported by the observation that loss of β-catenin blocks hair shaft formation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E,F).

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signaling suppresses Sox9 expression, which is important for hair follicle stem cell maintenance through inhibition of differentiation.
source: Also it suppresses Sox9 expression, which is important for HFSC maintenance through inhibition of differentiation (Kadaja et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 5 and citation to Kadaja et al., 2014.

claim: Embryonic exposure to Wnt/β-catenin signaling primes the embryonic cells for differentiation via both positive induction and lack of Sox9 expression, ultimately resulting in diminished long-term potential of the hair follicle stem cells.
source: So it is possible that embryonic exposure to Wnt/β-catenin signaling primes the embryonic cells for differentiation via both positive induction and lack of Sox9 expression. This ultimately results in diminished long-term potential of the HFSCs.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed differences in long-term potential.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signaling is necessary for hair follicle initiation.
source: Wnt/β-catenin signaling is necessary for HF initiation (Andl et al., 2002; Ito et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Early placode cells are Wnt/β-catenin signal responsive cells, and they generate all of the cells in adult hair follicles.
source: Early placode cells are Wnt/β-catenin signal responsive cells, and they generate all of the cells in adult HFs.
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing with Axin2-CreER mice and previous literature.

claim: At the hair peg stage, a localized Wnt/β-catenin signaling free zone emerges in upper hair follicle.
source: At the hair peg stage, a localized Wnt/β-catenin signaling free zone emerges in upper HF.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and TOPGAL reporter data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Progenitor cells residing in the Wnt/β-catenin signaling free zone stop further development and become hair follicle stem cells at the end of organogenesis.
source: Progenitor cells residing in this embryonic niche position stop further development and become HFSCs at the end of organogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing with Nfatc1-CreER mice shown in Figure 1.

claim: Established hair follicle stem cell precursor cells are not just remnants of embryonic progenitor cells, because they gain the expression of adult hair follicle stem cell markers including Nfatc1.
source: These established HFSC precursor cells are not just remnants of embryonic progenitor cells, because they gain the expression of adult HFSC markers including Nfatc1.
evidence: This is supported by the observation that Nfatc1 expression begins in hair peg.

claim: Embryonic cells residing in the Wnt/β-catenin signaling free zone, together with a few other cells located below them that have active Wnt/β-catenin signaling, give rise to the adult hair follicle stem cell pool.
source: Embryonic cells residing in this Wnt/β-catenin signaling free zone, together with a few other cells located below them that have active Wnt/β-catenin signaling, give rise to the adult HFSC pool.
evidence: This is a summary of the lineage tracing results from Axin2 and Sox9/Nfatc1 experiments.

claim: Only the hair follicle stem cells derived from Wnt/β-catenin signaling negative precursor cells have long-term self-renewal ability and can continuously support regeneration.
source: However, only the HFSCs derived from Wnt/β-catenin signaling negative precursor cells have long-term self-renewal ability and can continuously support regeneration.
evidence: This is supported by long-term lineage tracing shown in Figure 6.

claim: The small portion of hair follicle stem cells that are derived from embryonic cells with active Wnt/β-catenin signaling are highly prone to differentiation as the hair cycle progresses and are soon exhausted after regeneration.
source: The small portion of HFSCs that are derived from embryonic cells with active Wnt/β-catenin signaling are highly prone to differentiation as the hair cycle progresses and are soon exhausted after regeneration.
evidence: This is supported by long-term lineage tracing of Axin2+ cells shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In embryos, the attenuation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling not only defines the adult niche position and hair follicle stem cell fate, but also has a long lasting effect on the subsequent fate choice and long-term potential of cells in adults.
source: So, in embryos, the attenuation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling not only defines the adult niche position and HFSC fate, but also has a long lasting effect on the subsequent fate choice and long-term potential of cells in adults.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from all the experimental results.

claim: Lgr5+ and Axin2+ cells show largely non-overlapping labeling patterns in hair peg.
source: It's noteworthy that we observed largely none overlapping labeling patterns of Lgr5+ and Axin2+ cells in hair peg (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by imaging from lineage tracing experiments.

claim: Lgr5+ hair peg cells contributed hair follicle stem cells persist after multiple hair cycles instead of completely diminishing like Axin2+ cells contributed hair follicle stem cells.
source: Also, Lgr5+ hair peg cells contributed HFSCs persist after multiple hair cycles instead of completely diminishing like Axin2+ cells contributed HFSCs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by long-term lineage tracing shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In hair follicle, Lgr5 expression either reflects very low level of Wnt signaling, or it is induced by a different set of Wnt ligands than those that induce Axin2.
source: These results indicate it is possible that in hair follicle Lgr5 expression either reflects very low level of Wnt signaling, or it is induced by a different set of Wnt ligands than those induce Axin2.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the different patterns of Lgr5 and Axin2.

claim: Sox9 expression is induced by Shh signaling.
source: It has been reported previously that Sox9 expression is induced by Shh signaling (Vidal et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vidal et al., 2005.

claim: The mutually exclusive pattern of Sox9+ and Wnt/β-catenin signaling responsive cells can be explained by extended activity of Shh signaling throughout follicle epithelial cells and localized activity of Wnt/β-catenin signaling in lower follicle cells.
source: Given that we observed extended activity of Shh signaling throughout follicle epithelial cells and observed only localized activity of Wnt/β-catenin signaling in lower follicle cells, we can explain the mutually exclusive pattern of Sox9+ and Wnt/β-catenin signaling responsive cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed signaling patterns.

claim: As development proceeds, the Sox9 expression pattern continues to expand and become wider than the actual future bulge region; for example, Sox9 is expressed in most of the outer root sheath cells.
source: As development proceeds, the Sox9 expression pattern continues to expand and become wider than the actual future bulge region; for example, Sox9 is expressed in most of the ORS cells.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Following the emergence of the Wnt/β-catenin signaling free zone in the hair peg, there are probably other mechanisms that help maintain the restricted niche position.
source: So, following the emergence of the Wnt/β-catenin signaling free zone in the hair peg, there are probably other mechanisms that help maintain the restricted niche position.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observation that Sox9 expands beyond the niche.

claim: Once initiated in hair peg, the expression of Nfatc1 is restricted to the upper hair follicle where the future sebaceous gland and bulge will be; Nfatc1 expression does not expand to the broader outer root sheath like Sox9 expression does.
source: One observation further supporting this hypothesis is that, once initiated in hair peg, the expression of Nfatc1 is restricted to the upper HF where the future sebaceous gland and bulge will be; Nfatc1 expression does not expand to the broader ORS like Sox9 expression does.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Nfatc1 was reported to be a target of BMP signaling in adult hair follicles.
source: Nfatc1 was reported to be a target of BMP signaling in adult HFs (Horsley et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Horsley et al., 2008.

claim: Active BMP signaling was not observed at the hair peg niche location using a BMP reporter.
source: However, we did not observe active BMP signaling at the hair peg niche location using a BMP reporter, a result similar to a published staining pattern of pSMAD1/5 in developing HFs (Kandyba et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation and citation to Kandyba et al., 2014.

claim: Increased expression of Wnt inhibitors such as SFRPs was observed in Nfatc1+ hair peg cells as compared to Shh+ hair peg cells.
source: We observed increased expression of Wnt inhibitors such as SFRPs in Nfatc1+ hair peg cells as compared to Shh+ hair peg cells.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: It is unlikely that Wnt inhibitors expressed by the precursor cells themselves are the main causes of attenuated Wnt/β-catenin signaling in the hair peg niche position, given that hair follicle stem cell precursor cells can be replaced by embryonic cells occupying the same hair peg niche position.
source: However, given that HFSC precursor cells can be replaced by embryonic cells occupying the same hair peg niche position, it is unlikely that Wnt inhibitors expressed by the precursor cells themselves are the main causes of attenuated Wnt/β-catenin signaling in that position.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ablation experiments showing niche-dependent HFSC formation.

claim: RNA-seq analysis revealed enrichment of Wnt and Dkk expression in Wnt/β-catenin signal positive Shh+ hair peg cells as compared to Nfatc1+ hair peg cells.
source: Our RNA seq analysis revealed enrichment of Wnt and Dkk expression in Wnt/β-catenin signal positive Shh+ hair peg cells as compared to Nfatc1+ hair peg cells.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The combination of the lack of Wnt ligands, which are short-range signal molecules, and the presence of Wnt inhibitors such as DKK4, which are long-range signal molecules, at the embryonic niche location is hypothesized to be the main reason contributing to the emergence of a Wnt/β-catenin signaling free zone in upper hair peg.
source: We hypothesize that the combination of the lack of Wnt ligands, which are short-range signal molecules, and the presence of Wnt inhibitors such as DKK4, which are long-range signal molecules, at the embryonic niche location is the main reason contributes to the emergence of a Wnt/β-catenin signaling free zone in upper hair peg.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their data.

claim: A similar model combining short-range activators and long-range inhibitors has been used to explain hair follicle density determination and epidermal stem cell regulation.
source: A similar model has been used to explain HF density determination and epidermal SC regulation (Sick et al., 2006; Lim et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.
